description: We’re an international, multidisciplinary team bringing together UX/UI design, multimedia development, video production, marketing, and management. We love making complex ideas clear, creating intuitive experiences, and telling stories that connect with people. United by curiosity and a passion for space, we turn bold ideas into thoughtful designs and bring them to life!
summary:
ASTRUVI is an AI health assistant we are developing to help astronauts look after their health in space, especially when they cannot speak to a doctor on Earth straight away.

Our prototype asks how they feel, helps them record symptoms and prepares a clear summary for the medical team. We also propose connecting it to sensors and adding simple checks of hearing, balance, voice and facial movements.

To show how it could work, we follow a fictional astronaut who develops ear pain, dizziness and hearing loss. ASTRUVI helps her keep track of these changes and explain what is happening, with text and visual alerts if hearing becomes difficult.

The idea is simple: help astronauts notice when something is wrong and ask for help in time. ASTRUVI supports doctors but does not replace them. It is a demonstration prototype, and its medical features still need testing and validation.
details:
What does ASTRUVI do?

ASTRUVI is an AI health assistant concept that helps astronauts look after their health when they cannot speak to a doctor on Earth straight away. We developed an interactive prototype where they can record how they feel, describe symptoms and prepare a clear summary for medical review.

How does it work?

The astronaut starts with a simple check-in. They can describe how they feel emotionally, choose the affected body area, confirm the side and record when symptoms began. They can review and correct their answers before saving them locally.

Our demonstration follows Alexandra, a fictional astronaut who develops symptoms inspired by Ramsay Hunt syndrome, including ear pain, dizziness, tinnitus, hearing loss and facial weakness. Her story shows why recording changes and communicating clearly matters.

The interface includes text-based interaction and visible status messages, so it does not depend on hearing spoken instructions. Users can download a symptom summary. Sending it to a medical team is currently a clearly labelled simulation.

What are the benefits?

Our goal is to make reporting health problems easier, especially when someone feels worried, tired or has difficulty hearing. A clear record could help astronauts explain what has changed and give the medical team useful information to review. These benefits still need testing.

What do we hope to achieve?

We want to develop the prototype into a useful support tool for long missions. Future work would explore connecting sensors and adding guided checks of hearing, balance, voice and facial movements. These features would require medical input, implementation and clinical validation.

What did we use?

We used HTML, CSS and JavaScript to build the browser-based interface, with local browser storage for saved demo entries. No specialist hardware or live sensors are connected.

NASA health research and clinical decision-support resources informed the concept. ChatGPT helped with wording, interface code and fictional illustrations. The demonstration uses synthetic information rather than real astronaut medical records.

ASTRUVI supports doctors. It does not replace them.
